main.title: Transforming Designs into Code. Full-Stack Web Developer.
main.about: I’m Matvey, a Front-end & Full-Stack Developer with a strong focus on React, TypeScript, and modern web architectures. I build complex, scalable, and performance-oriented applications with a strong emphasis on user experience, clean architecture, and business logic. My background includes both frontend-heavy and full-stack projects, ranging from highly interactive UI platforms to large-scale systems with maps, payments, SEO, and role-based logic.

main.title: Front-end & Full-Stack Developer focused on scalable architectures, performance, and modern user experiences.
main.text1: My name is Matvey, and my journey in web development began in high school, where I first explored HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. By the 11th grade, I had built a strong foundation in frontend technologies, which led me to pursue a degree in Computer Engineering at Kharkiv National University of Radio Electronics. During my studies, I gained a solid understanding of core programming principles, including algorithms, data structures, and object-oriented programming, while working with languages such as Java and Python.
main.text2: Alongside my university education, I continued developing as a frontend engineer, mastering JavaScript, Git, and modern development workflows. I chose React as my primary framework and later expanded my expertise with TypeScript and Redux Toolkit. My professional career started with an internship at HARBOUR TECH ABI CRM LTD, where I worked on CRM systems for the Spanish market, handling bug fixes, UI improvements, and content updates using JavaScript, HTML, SCSS, and WordPress. After the internship, I was promoted to a Junior Frontend Developer position, where I gained my first commercial experience in a real Agile environment.
main.text3: Later, I joined Arctic Web, where I initially worked as a Frontend Developer and gradually evolved into a Full-Stack Developer. I built multiple projects from scratch, taking responsibility for architecture, UI implementation, complex client-side logic, animations, performance optimization, and later backend development using the MERN stack. I worked closely with technical leads, designers, and backend developers, and also independently delivered several complex platforms. Today, I focus on building scalable, maintainable systems with modern stacks such as Next.js and NestJS, continuously improving both my technical depth and product-oriented thinking.

workradar.text: Work Radar is a large-scale job search and recruitment platform focused on employment opportunities across Europe. The platform connects companies and recruiters with candidates, allowing businesses to publish job offers and services while candidates can explore vacancies, view locations on an interactive map, filter offers by distance and salary, and apply directly through the platform. Work Radar combines advanced geolocation features, flexible salary conversion, and strong SEO optimization to deliver a performant and user-friendly experience.
workradar.myRole:
I was fully responsible for the design, architecture, and development of the Work Radar platform as a full-stack developer. I implemented the entire front-end based on the provided design and later developed the complete back-end from scratch. My responsibilities included building a role-based system with two main user types (recruiters and candidates), implementing a multi-step authentication and registration flow (email/password, Google OAuth, and LinkedIn OAuth), and developing secure role-based route protection.

A significant part of my work focused on complex geolocation and map logic. I implemented an optimized interactive map with reusable markers, clustering overlapping points, and memoization to prevent unnecessary re-renders during filtering and searching. I also built logic for detecting user location via browser geolocation with fallback to IP-based location, persisting location data locally and synchronizing it with the database.

I designed and implemented advanced filtering and search logic based on user radius, geolocation, salary ranges, and multiple criteria, including infinite scrolling with lazy loading to avoid traditional pagination. Salary and currency conversion logic was built from scratch, supporting numeric ranges, string-based values, multiple currencies, cached exchange rates, and graceful fallbacks.

On the content side, I implemented rich text editing for job offers and services using Quill, preserving original HTML structure for correct rendering and SEO. I also developed a custom SSR-based SEO solution on the back-end to ensure proper meta tags, images, and previews when sharing job offers or services.

Additionally, I built a full-featured admin panel that allows administrators to manage users, offers, services, and applications, including activation, deactivation, deletion, and content moderation. Admins can export user data to Excel, manage platform content, and monitor activity. I also implemented scheduled tasks using cron jobs to automatically remove expired job offers.

Overall, I designed the entire system architecture, coordinated technical decisions with the technical director, optimized performance across the application, and delivered the project fully on time. Work Radar is one of my most complex and complete projects, combining front-end, back-end, optimization, SEO, and advanced business logic into a single scalable platform.

trepco.text: Trepco is a B2B wholesale ordering platform for Trepco, a large US distributor serving convenience stores, grocery and liquor stores, smoke shops and hospitality businesses across two divisions — Trepco West (Southern California and Nevada) and Trepco Mid-West (Michigan, Indiana and Ohio). Retail customers sign in with their customer number, browse a division-specific catalogue with their own negotiated prices, choose units of measure, delivery or warehouse pickup, and place orders that go straight into Trepco's ERP through the ForceField4 (Jargon) middleware — without anyone re-keying them by hand. Products, stock, customers, prices and order statuses stay synchronised with the ERP automatically, while division administrators manage customers, invitations, orders, catalogue content and order rules from a dedicated admin panel.
trepco.myRole:
I led Trepco end to end as a full-stack developer — from the monorepo architecture and the NestJS back-end to the Next.js front-end, the ERP integration, the admin panel and deployment. The platform is a pnpm + Turborepo monorepo with two deployable apps: a modular NestJS 10 API of 16 feature modules and more than 80 endpoints backed by 20 MongoDB collections, and a Next.js 16 application with a feature-sliced architecture covering the marketing site, the division entrance, the customer portal and the admin area.

The core of the project is the integration with ForceField4 — the ERP middleware that owns products, stock, customers, prices and orders. I built a layered client from scratch: an HTTP transport with retries and timeouts, a session manager that logs in per division, caches the session and re-authenticates transparently on expiry, and an API client that normalises the ERP's responses. Each division works against its own ERP dataset, and the browser never talks to the ERP directly — every call goes through the API.

The most complex part is order placement. Before checkout, a validation engine builds a prepared checkout snapshot: it refreshes personal prices, clamps quantities to real availability, converts units of measure, resolves which warehouse can serve the customer by delivery or pickup, enforces tobacco licence rules for California and Nevada and checks per-division order minimums for tobacco and non-tobacco subtotals — all money is calculated in cents. If anything changed, the customer sees exactly what and confirms it. The order itself is exported through an idempotent state machine — verify customer → create draft → save lines → verify saved lines against the validated checkout → close — with concurrency guards, safe retries that resume from the last completed step, an explicit "uncertain" state for ERP timeouts that require reconciliation, and a final MongoDB transaction that updates availability, syncs the cart and sends the confirmation e-mail.

I also designed the background synchronisation that keeps the portal in step with the ERP: a scheduler that, per division, syncs customers (and automatically sends invitations to new ones), products and stock, categories, product images (downloaded from the ERP and stored in AWS S3 with controlled concurrency and size limits) and the fulfilment and invoice status of exported orders. It is safe to run on several replicas thanks to distributed locks with TTLs in MongoDB, every run is recorded in a visible sync history, and customers who subscribed to a product receive back-in-stock e-mails automatically. Personal prices are fetched in batches and cached for 72 hours.

Customers do not self-register: I implemented an invitation-based onboarding where the customer is created in the ERP, synchronised into the portal and receives a single-use invitation stored as a SHA-256 hash with a limited lifetime; password reset works the same way. Authentication uses JWT and bcrypt, and the role model includes customers, a global admin and division-scoped admins whose access is enforced on the server for every query.

On top of that I built a full admin panel — dashboard, users and invitations, ERP customers, orders with exports to Excel, product and category management, home slider images, order minimums and sync controls — plus PDF order acknowledgements rendered with Puppeteer, transactional e-mails through Brevo and saved products with availability alerts for customers. The code base is covered by nearly 80 Jest test suites, formatted and linted with Biome and deployed with Coolify. Trepco is one of my most integration-heavy projects: a production B2B commerce platform where every order has to land in the ERP correctly, exactly once.

leoai.text: LeoAI is an AI-powered assistant for UK employment law built for HR decision-makers, solicitors and case workers. Users describe a workplace situation to Leo — an AI agent running on Azure AI Foundry — and receive streamed, fully cited answers grounded in UK legislation, employment tribunal and appeal decisions, case law and official guidance from sources such as legislation.gov.uk, the National Archives, ACAS and the EHRC. Beyond the chat, the platform guides a matter from start to finish: users open a case, upload documents and e-mails, build the facts, see legal risks, receive an action plan, draft documents, keep an auditable record and escalate when needed. It supports group chats where Leo joins on mention, shared workspaces with roles and invitations, voice input, multi-format attachments with OCR, automatic archiving and long-term retention, exportable audit logs and strong account security with two-factor authentication — all running on a production Azure infrastructure in the UK.
leoai.myRole:
I worked on LeoAI as a full-stack developer in a small engineering team, owning several of the most complex parts of the product across the NestJS API, the Next.js front-end and the AI layer. The platform is a pnpm + Turborepo monorepo of three independently deployed services — the web app, the core API with around 100 REST endpoints and 26 Prisma models on PostgreSQL with pgvector, and a dedicated MCP retrieval server — deployed to Azure App Service through GitHub Actions.

On the AI side, I built the integration of the conversation flow with Azure AI Foundry: an AI-first conversation pipeline where the Foundry agent keeps the dialogue server-side, persisted Foundry sessions and sources, and a per-chat legal "matter state" that tracks the stage of the case, facts, fact gaps, risk flags and escalation to independent legal advice. I implemented matter gates and response validation, locking conversations to the selected employment-law category, citation handling that turns the agent's retrieval tool calls into source references, and request tracing with sanitisation of citation markers in the streamed output.

On the front-end, I built the core chat experience: streamed AI responses with Markdown rendering, citation chips grouped by paragraph with de-duplicated sources, message actions and client-side request tracing, and I documented the chat UX contracts and streaming workflows for the team.

I then delivered the Cases module end to end — case domain and ownership-scoped conversations, a secure Azure Blob-backed document lifecycle, a processing pipeline that extracts text from uploaded files including Outlook .msg e-mails, splits it into chunks, creates embeddings and injects the most relevant fragments into Leo's context, plus bulk uploads with pre-flight validation, case metadata as context, pinning, archiving and permanent deletion, and the full set of case screens in the interface.

In the production-hardening phase I led the API security work: global deny-by-default authentication with explicit public routes, configurable rate limiting per user and IP, upload limits enforced before files are buffered, production-safe CORS and API documentation settings, and a strictly typed authorization context, together with restoring the full test suite in CI. I also wrote the product knowledge base for the project, set up the AI-assisted development workflow for the monorepo and built animated, responsive sections of the marketing landing page. LeoAI is one of the most technically advanced products I have worked on: an agentic RAG system with a custom MCP server, real-time streaming, strict data retention and an enterprise-grade Azure cloud setup.

contrify.text: Contrify is a B2B SaaS platform for the German real-estate market that helps property managers, owner associations (WEG) and building owners take control of what they pay for elevator maintenance, repairs and mandatory safety inspections (ZÜS). A customer simply uploads a maintenance contract, a repair offer or an inspection report — as a PDF, a scan or a phone photo — and AI reads it, extracting the provider, prices, contract dates, notice periods and defects. Contrify then sends anonymised requests to service providers in the region, collects their offers through secure links or plain e-mail replies, normalises and scores them, and produces a clear comparison report. When the customer picks a better offer, the platform handles the entire switch end to end: power of attorney, digital or manual signing, passing the order to the new provider, tracking the cancellation deadline of the old contract and following up until every confirmation is in. It is a complex, legally sensitive product where money, deadlines and contracts all have to be exactly right.
contrify.myRole:
I was responsible for Contrify end to end as a full-stack developer — from the architecture and database design to the AI pipeline, payments, integrations, the admin area and deployment. The product is one large Next.js 16 application that combines the customer app, the staff area, a public marketing site, a provider-facing response portal and a REST API of more than 140 endpoints, backed by over 130 domain services and a PostgreSQL schema of roughly 50 tables built through 46 hand-written SQL migrations.

I built the document intelligence pipeline: uploads of PDFs, scans and photos (including HEIC from iPhones) are stored in Cloudflare R2, pre-processed and passed through an asynchronous OCR worker, then analysed by OpenAI GPT-4o (text and vision) to extract structured contract data, prices, deadlines and inspection defects. Personal data is redacted before it ever reaches the model, every AI call is logged with its cost, and the flow is designed so that uploading is free while parsing is a paid action protected by an entitlement system.

I designed the outreach and comparison engine: anonymised German requests are sent to providers in the region, providers answer through a tokenised public page or simply by replying to the e-mail (inbound e-mail is parsed and attached to the right request automatically), and incoming offers are normalised and scored by a configurable weighted model. Comparison reports are generated as PDF, Excel and CSV — always in German, because they are presented at owners' meetings as the basis for formal decisions.

The most demanding part was the switching and contract lifecycle. I implemented a company-wide power of attorney (Vollmacht) as its own step, order signing either manually or through DocuSign (integrated directly over REST with JWT authentication, without an SDK), release of the order to the new provider with automatic reminders and escalation, and a contract lifecycle engine that calculates cancellation deadlines with exact calendar-month arithmetic in the Europe/Berlin timezone, renews auto-renewing contracts nightly, sends end-of-term reminders and tracks ZÜS inspection deadlines. All of it runs on a nightly job and webhooks that are built to be idempotent, so retries and duplicate events never corrupt data.

I also built the full billing system on Stripe with two business models — pay-per-request and a yearly subscription per elevator — including a money-back guarantee with a 21-day search window, a refund queue with working-day deadlines, promo vouchers and grandfathered accounts. Stripe and DocuSign webhooks work as ledgers: events are stored first and reconciled, so replays always converge to the correct state.

Security and compliance were a priority from day one: custom session-based authentication with HTTP-only cookies, rate limiting, strict multi-tenant isolation by company, a role model with customers, admins and superadmins, a full audit log of every staff action, configurable data-retention policies and GDPR data export and account deletion. On top of that I built a staff area with platform metrics, company and user management, the provider catalogue, AI logs, service health and editable e-mail templates, an idempotent in-app notification center, and full German/English localisation.

To keep such a large system reliable, I wrote nearly 200 self-checking guard scripts that verify business rules against a real database — pricing consistency, deadline calculations, billing flows, tenant isolation and more — and set up the deployment on a VPS with nginx, system cron and Sentry monitoring. Contrify is the most complex product I have built so far: a real end-to-end SaaS that combines AI, payments, e-signatures, legal deadlines and multi-tenant architecture in one scalable platform.
descriptionText: Next.js 16 (App Router), React 19 & TypeScript: One full-stack application that hosts the customer app, the staff area, the marketing site, the provider portal and a REST API of 140+ endpoints with strict typing end to end.

Supabase (PostgreSQL): Around 50 tables with row-level security, multi-tenant isolation by company and 46 idempotent SQL migrations — deliberately without an ORM for full control over queries and schema.
OpenAI GPT-4o (text & vision): AI extraction of contract data, prices, deadlines and inspection defects from PDFs, scans and photos, with PII redaction and per-call cost logging.
Asynchronous OCR pipeline: Background worker with job queue, image pre-processing and HEIC conversion for reliable recognition of real-world documents.
Stripe: Pay-per-request and yearly per-unit subscription billing, checkout, vouchers, a money-back guarantee with refund workflow and ledger-style idempotent webhooks.
DocuSign (REST + JWT): Digital signing of powers of attorney and orders, integrated directly over the REST API without an SDK, with webhook reconciliation against live envelope status.
Resend: Transactional e-mail and inbound e-mail processing — providers can answer requests simply by replying to the e-mail, with delivery tracking for every message.
Cloudflare R2 (S3 API): Secure storage of contracts, offers and reports with signed URLs and controlled access per company.
PDF, Excel & CSV generation (React-PDF, pdf-lib, ExcelJS): German comparison reports, order documents and powers of attorney generated on the server.
next-intl: Full German/English localisation with ICU plurals; everything providers see and every report is always in German.
Tailwind CSS, Radix UI & shadcn/ui: Accessible, responsive and consistent interface for a data-heavy B2B product.
React Hook Form, Zod & SWR: Complex validated forms and a typed client data layer with caching and revalidation.
Security & GDPR: Session-based auth with HTTP-only cookies and bcrypt, rate limiting, audit logging, data-retention policies, GDPR export and account deletion.
VPS, nginx, cron & Sentry: Self-hosted deployment with a nightly job for deadlines and renewals, plus error monitoring in production.
Guard scripts: Nearly 200 self-checking scripts that verify billing, deadlines, isolation and other business rules against a real database.

legal-platform.text: Legal Platform is an AI-powered tool for lawyers that generates global equity-compensation legal memoranda — detailed documents that explain what a company must do to grant employee equity awards (stock options, RSUs, ESPP, token awards and more) in specific countries. A lawyer selects up to 10 of 54 supported countries, the award types and the type of worker (employee, EOR or PEO employee, contractor), either through a conversational AI chat or a structured step-by-step wizard, and within minutes receives a fully formatted, editable Word memorandum covering labour law, foreign exchange control, data privacy, taxation, social insurance, withholding and reporting, translation and electronic signature requirements for every selected country. Because legal content must never be invented, the platform is built around a strict grounded-generation pipeline: every sentence in the memo is taken from approved legal source documents, validated in code and traceable back to its source.
legal-platform.myRole:
I built Legal Platform end to end as practically the sole developer — the React front-end, the Node.js/Express API, the RAG pipeline, the document-generation engine, authentication and deployment. Over roughly a year I designed the architecture, implemented every feature and iterated on it directly with the client's lawyers, turning their annotated feedback on real memoranda into code and regression tests.

The heart of the project is a self-built retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system that runs without a vector database. Approved legal DOCX sources are stored in AWS S3, embedded with OpenAI text-embedding-3-small in token-aware batches, and indexed as JSON in S3 with an in-memory cache and cosine-similarity top-K retrieval. I later built a second-generation structured indexing pipeline: DOCX structure extraction, LLM-based classification of every source by country, section, award type and worker type, section-aware chunking with overlap, per-country indexes, incremental re-indexing based on S3 ETags and content hashes, and an atomic publish process that only switches the live index once a full build has completed. Strategy flags allow a safe rollout with fallback to the legacy index, and the whole indexing flow is managed through a dedicated CLI.

The most important engineering challenge was making AI output legally trustworthy. I designed an extractive, hallucination-proof generation pipeline: the model may only reuse sentences from retrieved source excerpts, each tagged with its source file, and every generated sentence is then verified in code against the source corpus by exact match or high token overlap. If validation fails, generation retries in a stricter mode, and if information is genuinely missing, a fixed safe text is used instead of an invented one. On top of that I built scope isolation for multi-country and multi-award memos, which detects and removes content that does not belong to the selected awards or worker types, together with a per-section grounding audit stored in S3 and a Source Transparency panel that shows lawyers exactly which documents each section was built from.

For document output, I built a template-driven rendering engine on docxtemplater that fills the firm's own memorandum template with single- or multi-country content — ordered country sections, a cover and introduction extracted from source documents, consistent legal terminology, bold action items and correct formatting — producing a Word file that lawyers can continue editing. Generated memos are stored in S3 with metadata in MongoDB and are available in a document library with search, filtering, renaming, deletion and an in-browser DOCX preview.

On the user-experience side, I implemented two generation modes: an AI chat with a typed conversational intake that extracts countries, awards and worker types from free text and asks for confirmation, and a four-step form wizard. Generation is streamed in real time over Server-Sent Events with typed progress events and per-country tracking, handles client disconnects, protects against concurrent generations and continues as a pending job with background polling for long runs. I also implemented JWT authentication, admin-only account management with roles, search and filters, per-user generation limits, and the CI/CD pipeline with GitHub Actions deploying to a VPS managed by PM2.

The back-end is fully typed, with no `any`, central type guards and typed SSE contracts, and is covered by around 100 Jest test cases for scope isolation, source selection, terminology, multi-country ordering and template rendering. Legal Platform is one of my most advanced AI projects: a production RAG system where accuracy, traceability and trust matter more than anything else.

Tailwind CSS, Radix UI & Framer Motion: Accessible, responsive interface with smooth animations and real-time progress UI.
Node.js, Express & TypeScript: REST API with typed controllers, middleware-based JWT auth and role checks, and Zod validation.
MongoDB (Mongoose): Users and generated documents with metadata, audit trails and optimised compound and multikey indexes.
OpenAI (GPT-4o family & text-embedding-3-small): Conversational parameter extraction, document classification, embeddings and grounded section generation.
Custom RAG engine: Embeddings, token-aware batching, cosine top-K retrieval and recency-first ranking, implemented without a vector database.
Structured RAG v2 indexing: LLM classification, section-aware chunking, per-country indexes, incremental re-indexing and atomic index publishing.
Extractive generation & provenance validation: Every sentence is verified against source excerpts, with strict-mode retries and safe fallbacks.
Server-Sent Events (SSE): Real-time streaming of generation progress with typed events and multi-country tracking.
docxtemplater, PizZip, docx & Mammoth: Template-based Word memorandum rendering and DOCX parsing of legal sources.
AWS S3: Storage for legal sources, generated memoranda, RAG indexes and audit artifacts, with presigned download URLs.
JWT & bcrypt: Secure authentication with admin-managed accounts and role-based access.

GitHub Actions, VPS & PM2: Automated deployment pipeline with process management on a virtual server.

british-hills.text: British Hills is an interactive multi-page web platform for an English language school, designed to attract and onboard new students. The website allows users to submit enrollment requests and complete an interactive English level test, with results and contact details sent directly to administrators for further processing. The platform focuses on engagement, accessibility, and a visually rich user experience.
british-hills.myRole: I was fully responsible for the front-end development of the British Hills platform, implementing the complete user interface based on the provided design. sps.text: Smart Property Systems is a property-management software company whose platform connects staff, tenants, vendors, agents and owners through five purpose-built portals sharing one accounting engine — covering accounting, repairs and maintenance, inspections, vacancy marketing, document management, reporting and integrated payments. I worked on the company's product website: a fully CMS-driven Next.js platform managed in Sanity, with a transparent per-unit pricing calculator, product, solutions and FAQ pages, analytics and cookie consent. Its centrepiece is Grace — an AI assistant built into the site that answers visitors' questions about the product in natural language, in any language, by text or by voice, grounded strictly in the content the marketing team manages in the CMS.
sps.myRole:
I joined Smart Property Systems after the initial layout was built, to take over the complex logic: the AI assistant, the integrations and the CMS-driven features. Over the following weeks I designed and implemented Grace end to end — the back-end pipeline, the knowledge system, the voice layer, the chat interface logic and the content model in Sanity.

On the server, I built Grace's chat pipeline on top of the Anthropic Claude Messages API: request validation, a cached knowledge snapshot, and a system prompt assembled from separate blocks — language rules, behaviour settings from the CMS, the assistant's role, retrieved knowledge and the context of the button that opened the chat. Calls are protected with timeouts, retries with backoff on rate limits and server errors, typed error codes and a fallback reply configured by editors. The API is protected by proxy-aware rate limiting that trusts client IP headers only when the hosting provider is confirmed.

The most interesting part was the knowledge and retrieval system, built without a vector database. A pipeline collects content from all CMS pages in parallel, converts it into a set of plain facts and caches it with tag-based revalidation, so Grace always answers from up-to-date content. Retrieval works in two stages: a fast lexical scoring step shortlists FAQ and fact candidates, boosted by the page the visitor is on and the pages they visited, and then Claude selects the best match across languages and returns structured JSON with a confidence score. Grace detects the language of every message, remembers an explicit language preference during the session and translates canonical answers without changing their meaning.

I also made the assistant fully manageable from the CMS: I designed the "Grace Knowledge" content model in Sanity — settings, FAQ entries with synonyms and priorities, instructions and do/don't rules — so the marketing team can switch Grace on or off and change its tone, reply length, fallback text and hard rules without a deployment. For voice, I integrated OpenAI text-to-speech with strictly typed, allow-listed settings and built browser playback with a careful audio lifecycle and cancellation handling.

I also built an AI lead-qualification flow that extracted contact details, portfolio size and current software from a free-form conversation using a combination of pattern matching and LLM extraction, validated them and submitted them server-side to the HubSpot CRM with de-duplication and delayed submission; the client later decided to keep Grace as a pure knowledge assistant, and I removed the flow cleanly. Beyond the assistant, I implemented context-aware buttons across the site that open Grace with a specific goal, with cooldowns and auto-open rules that respect the cookie banner, plus new Sanity-driven features — a comparison table section, a contact modal that routes visitors by portfolio size, a coming-soon flow and a favicon managed in the CMS — Google Analytics 4 with route-level page-view tracking, and a number of responsive and hydration fixes.
descriptionText: Next.js 16 (App Router), React 19 & TypeScript: CMS-driven marketing platform with server-side API routes for the AI assistant and strict typing throughout.
Sanity (headless CMS): Embedded Sanity Studio, GROQ queries and page-builder sections, plus a custom "Grace Knowledge" content model for managing the assistant without deployments.
Anthropic Claude (Messages API): Conversational replies, cross-language answer selection and structured JSON outputs with confidence scores.
Custom two-stage retrieval: Lexical candidate scoring with page-context boosts followed by LLM re-ranking — implemented without a vector database.
Knowledge pipeline: Parallel collection of all CMS content into a cached fact snapshot with tag-based revalidation.
OpenAI Text-to-Speech: Voice replies with typed, allow-listed voice, format and speed settings and managed browser playback.
HubSpot Forms API: Server-side submission of AI-qualified leads with typed field mapping and de-duplication.
Google Analytics 4: Route-level page-view tracking and typed event helpers.
Tailwind CSS v4 & react-markdown: Responsive chat interface with Markdown rendering of AI replies.
Rate limiting & resilience: Proxy-aware per-IP sliding-window limits, timeouts, retries with backoff and editor-defined fallbacks.
Docker & Coolify: Containerised multi-stage builds and deployment.

It provides an immersive 3D experience, interactive trading features, and informative sections such as the About and Investment pages. The project combines modern UI design with blockchain integration to deliver a professional and engaging user experience.
daiwo.myRole: My role in the DAIWO project involved optimizing performance and refactoring existing components to improve efficiency and maintainability. Additionally, I implemented the full logic for the Investment System page — including staking mechanics, percentage calculations, wallet connection integration, and interactive state management with accordions and user actions. Overall, my focus was on improving usability, interactivity, and code performance across the platform.
